title: Khoresh-e mast
subtitle: Persian yoghurt and lamb stew with saffron and rose water
excerpt: Khoresh-e mast is an unusual Persian stew of very slowly braised lamb in a thick yoghurt sauce with saffron and a hint of rose water. The yoghurt is stabilised with egg yolk before going in so it doesn't split during the long cook. The result is mild, creamy, and fragrant.
sourceNotes: Najmieh Batmanglij, Food of Life: Ancient Persian and Modern Iranian Cooking and Ceremonies (1986). Khoresh-e mast documented as a traditional Isfahan dish, one of the more unusual and elegant khoresh. Margaret Shaida, The Legendary Cuisine of Persia (1992). Notes on the yoghurt stabilisation technique and the use of rose water.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The braised lamb can be cooked up to two days ahead. Add the stabilised yoghurt on the day and heat gently.

content.text: Khoresh-e mast is a Persian yoghurt stew from Isfahan: braised lamb in a saffron-scented yoghurt sauce finished with rose water. The yoghurt is stabilised with an egg yolk so it does not curdle during cooking, giving a silky, creamy sauce around the tender lamb. The rose water keeps it subtle; the saffron gives colour and depth. Serve over chelow.

items.prepNote: ground, dissolved in 3 tbsp hot water
yolks only, to stabilise the yoghurt

content.text: Heat {{olive-oil}} in a heavy pot over medium-high heat. Add {{onion}} and cook for fifteen minutes until deeply golden. Add {{turmeric-ground}} and {{cinnamon-ground}} and stir for one minute.

Add {{lamb-shoulder}} and brown well on all sides. Pour in half the dissolved {{saffron}} and 300 ml of water. Season with {{sea-salt-fine}}. Bring to the boil, then reduce to a low simmer, cover, and cook for 60 to 70 minutes until the lamb is very tender.
Whisk {{plain-yoghurt}} with the two egg yolks from {{eggs}}, the remaining {{saffron}} water, and {{rose-water}} until smooth.

Remove the pot from the heat and let the lamb cool slightly for five minutes. Add the yoghurt mixture to the pot and stir gently to combine. Return to the lowest possible heat and cook uncovered for fifteen to twenty minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens to a coating consistency. Do not boil.
Taste and adjust salt. Serve over chelow with {{pine-nuts}} scattered over if using.

items.symptom: The yoghurt has split and the sauce looks grainy
items.cause: Heat too high after adding the yoghurt
items.fix: The yoghurt must never boil. Keep the heat at the lowest setting and stir frequently. The egg yolks stabilise but only at gentle heat.

items.symptom: The rose water flavour is too strong
items.cause: Rose water concentration varies significantly by brand
items.fix: Add in two stages: half first, taste, then decide if more is needed. The rose should be a background note, not the dominant flavour.

items.cause: Yoghurt had a high water content
items.fix: Strain the yoghurt through muslin for an hour before using to remove excess liquid. Or reduce the braising liquid further before adding the yoghurt.

items.symptom: The lamb is tough after the braise
items.fix: Lamb shoulder can take 80 to 90 minutes at a low simmer to become fully tender. Give it more time before adding the yoghurt.

content.text: Khoresh-e mast is from central Iran, linked to Isfahan, a city known for refined cooking. The yoghurt and rose water are typical of Persian cooking's use of floral scents in both savoury and sweet dishes. It is one of the more unusual khoresh: the pale, creamy sauce is quieter than tomato-forward or herb-heavy stews. The flavour is mild and almost delicate, which makes it a good choice for a special meal. The pine nuts add texture and richness that works well with the yoghurt.
